title: Why We Ghost
body: Ghosting used to be rude. Now it is normal. People stop replying because a real conversation feels too heavy. But the person on the other side never learns what went wrong.

title: Why We're Bad at Small Talk
body:
Small talk gets a bad reputation. Most people say they hate it, yet almost everyone does it every day. The problem is not the weather or the traffic; it is the fear of saying something boring. So we keep the conversation on safe ground, and it dies in a few sentences.

Researchers who study conversation found something simple: people enjoy talking about themselves far more than they expect to. A question like "what was the best part of your week" works better than "how are you", because it asks for a story instead of a status report.

The goal of small talk is not to impress anyone. It is to find one thing worth following up on, and then follow up on it.

title: The Hidden Cost of Delivery
body:
Ordering food has never been easier. A few taps, and dinner arrives in twenty minutes. What the app does not show you is the full price: the menu is often marked up, the delivery fee changes with the weather, and there is a service charge that appears only at checkout.

For restaurants, the platform takes a cut of every order. Some owners raise menu prices on the app to cover it, which means the customer pays twice: once for the food, once for the convenience.

None of this means you should delete the app. It means you should compare. Walking to the place nearby is sometimes cheaper and faster than waiting for a courier to cross the city in traffic.

title: Learning to Say No
body:
Saying no is a skill, and most of us learn it late. As students we say yes to every club, every group project, every invitation. Later at work, the same habit turns into extra shifts and unfinished tasks that belong to someone else.

The trick is not to become rude. It is to be clear and quick. "I can't take this on this week" is a complete sentence. You do not owe anyone a long explanation, and a vague "maybe later" usually costs more than an honest no, because it keeps the other person waiting.

People who say no well are not less liked. They are simply more predictable, and being predictable is what makes trust possible.
